generalizedRange: Eastern and southern Africa — Namibia, South Africa, Kenya, Zimbabwe and a handful of other range states
hook: In 1970, some 65,000. By 1993, about 2,300. The count climbs again.

story.text: The black rhino is a browser: a hooked, prehensile upper lip pulls leaves and thorny branches into its mouth.
Its two horns — the front up to four feet — are keratin, thousands of compressed strands of the stuff of fingernails.
In 1970 there were about 65,000; by 1993 poaching for that horn had cut them to some 2,300, a loss of 96 percent.
One of four subspecies did not survive: the western black rhino, last seen in Cameroon in 2003, was declared extinct in 2011.
In Namibia's Kunene, fewer than 40 remained in Damaraland by 1982, fewer than 10 in Kaokoland.
Today more than 60 rhino rangers from 13 community conservancies walk its 25,000 square kilometers in 20-day patrols, every sighting reported to the Ministry.
Rhinos in high-risk areas are dehorned or moved to safer ground; Namibia now holds more than a third of Africa's black rhinos.
The market has not gone away: South Africa lost 420 rhinos to poachers in 2024, with horn still moving toward Malaysia and Viet Nam.
The 2024 count stood at 6,788, up 5.2 percent in a year, at Africa's lowest poaching rate since 2011.
To witness the black rhino is to walk a while with the rangers — and to remember the fourth subspecies no one will count again.

reproduction.text: A single calf after fifteen to seventeen months, roughly one every two and a half to three years, and it stays with its mother for two to four years before she turns it away.

insight.text: A black rhino can go up to five days without drinking — and Kunene's desert rhinos live on a staple plant that is deadly to most other mammals, humans included.

programs.title: Rhino Ranger Programme, Kunene
programs.summary: Tracks Kunene's desert-adapted black rhinos on foot with rangers from the community conservancies, mentoring them on patrol and keeping a photographic life-history record of every animal.

programs.title: Lowveld rhino program, Zimbabwe
programs.summary: With the Lowveld Rhino Trust, monitors Zimbabwe's black rhinos daily, treats poaching injuries, and moves animals out of high-risk areas — the Lowveld conservancies hold about 90 percent of the country's rhinos.
